title: Hallelujah Chorus
description: Handel's Hallelujah chorus from Messiah, for 4 singers, in his own four voice parts as Ebenezer Prout's 1902 edition prints them, without the orchestra. Sung whole, a major third lower than printed so each part sits near a beginner's range: the Hallelujahs, the quiet "The kingdom of this world", the voices coming in one by one on "And He shall reign", and the sopranos' long notes climbing through "King of Kings".

credits.words: Charles Jennens's words for Messiah, from Revelation 19:6, 11:15 and 19:16 (King James Version)
credits.arrangement: Handel's own four voice parts (Prout's edition, 1902), adapted by Stackapella

licence.words: public domain: Charles Jennens, who wrote the words of Messiah (Dictionary of National Biography, 1885 to 1900, "Jennens, Charles", by Gordon Goodwin: "He also wrote the words for Handel's 'Saul' (1735), 'Messiah' (1742)"; "died unmarried on 20 Nov. 1773"), set from Revelation 19:6, 11:15 and 19:16 in the King James Version (1611), in Jennens's wording as Prout's edition prints it; in the UK the King James Version is under Crown letters patent (a question with our lawyer, as for The Lord Bless You)
licence.tune: public domain: Handel died 1759; the title page of Prout's edition says Messiah was "composed in the year 1741"
licence.arrangement: Handel's own four voice parts as Ebenezer Prout's edition prints them (Novello, 1902; Prout died 1909; public domain), every pitch and word as printed but for the changes named here, sung without the orchestra: the three bars of orchestral introduction are left out, so the song starts at the choir's first "Hallelujah" (bar 4), and every bar the choir sings is kept, its two short rests for all four parts too (three beats before "The kingdom of this world", two before the last "Hallelujah"). A major third lower than printed (B-flat for D), so each part sits near a beginner's range; tempo 60 (Prout prints crotchet = 72), the fastest at which Handel's quaver rests are a breath and his semiquaver "Hal-le" a quarter of a second. Prout's restored underlay is kept: "jah, Hal-" on one note in the alto (bar 24), soprano (bar 30) and bass (bars 31 and 32), and the tenor's "and He shall reign, and He shall reign" (bars 70 and 71). At bars 46 and 79 Prout prints a small lower D under the alto's top D; the alto sings the top note. Breaths written in for beginners, each taken from the end of a line's last note: before "reigneth" in each "for the Lord God Omnipotent reigneth"; after "become" and "Lord" and at the comma after the first "Christ" of "is become the Kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and of His Christ;" in every part; before "for" in each "and He shall reign for ever and ever"; before each "King of Kings" that follows "ever"; and the long "Kings" and "Lords" held a beat to four beats less (no line over 9 seconds), "world" (bar 35) a beat less in every part. The tenor's "for" at bars 25 and 29 starts half a beat late, after a breath (Handel's "Hallelujah!" runs into it on a quaver). The alto's octave drop on "Om-" (bars 18 and 30) stays on the upper note: a semitone under the app's lowest alto note in this key. Accepted exceptions (singable.py), all Handel's own writing in this key: rule 4, the soprano's low B-flat and C ("Om-" in bar 13, "this world is become" in bars 34 to 37, "for ever" in bars 72 to 74, up to 6 seconds at the bottom of the range) and its top F once ("He", bar 49), and its held D and E-flat on the climbing "King of Kings" and "Lord of Lords" (bars 63 to 68, 7.5 and 8.5 seconds at the top of the range); the alto's low F ("eth," bar 14; "jah," bar 25), the tenor's low B-flat ("Om-" bars 13 and 26, "eth," bar 19, "dom" bar 34) and the bass's low E-flat ("Om-" bar 18); rule 5, the alto's, tenor's and bass's slurs (Handel's melismas on "Hal-le", "be-come", "our", "ev-er" and "reign"), the octave leaps of "God Om-ni-po-tent" in every part and the leaps of the subject of "And He shall reign"; rule C, the parallel octaves and doubled leading notes of Handel's unison and octave passages ("for the Lord God Omnipotent reigneth", bars 12 to 14, 17 to 19, 25 to 27 and 29 to 31), the tenor above the alto in bars 28, 31, 38 and 50 and the bass above the tenor in bars 14 and 68.
